abstract: PSEN1 variants are the most common cause of familial early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD), but it is debated whether they act through a loss- or gain-of-function. Following a recent report of a duo with EOAD carrying a predicted loss-of-function (LoF) stop-gain variant (p.K109*) in PSEN1, we sought to determine whether PSEN1 LoF variants, as a class, cause EOAD. We identified 45 carriers of PSEN1 LoF variants predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay in the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project, UK Biobank, and BioVU databases. None of these carriers had a recorded case of early-onset dementia, and 17 were older than 65 years at last follow-up with no dementia or AD reported. Re-analysis of the reported AD-associated variant p.K109* revealed a cryptic splice site predicted to produce an in-frame deletion of 5 amino acids (p.K109_L113del). These results suggest that PSEN1 variants must produce an altered PSEN1 protein product to cause EOAD, while true null LoF PSEN1 alleles do not cause EOAD.
hook: Knocking out PSEN1 does not cause early-onset Alzheimer's. Only altered proteins do.
summary: Researchers searched three large genetic databases and found 45 people carrying PSEN1 variants predicted to destroy the gene's product, none with early-onset dementia. A reported case variant turned out to cause a small in-frame deletion instead. The carriers are few and mostly one-copy, and many were still young at last follow-up.
title: PSEN1 loss-of-function variants do not cause early-onset Alzheimer's disease
